evidence: Library of Congress western mining history
note: Nevada's nineteenth-century mining boom is a specific case of the broader western mineral-rush pattern: mineral discoveries drew migrants, capital and services, created boomtowns, and reorganized local economies. The hierarchy lets Twain's Nevada experience remain specific without making it a one-author universal category.
source_label: Library of Congress — Mining in the West

note: The Klondike stampede is another specific resource-boom frontier case: a gold discovery triggered mass migration, boomtown growth, service economies, environmental change, and intensified interaction with Indigenous and First Nations communities.
source_label: National Park Service — The Klondike Gold Rush as a migration event

note: U.S. territorial expansion, transport, state formation, and migration created conditions for rapid town-building, farming, ranching, and other settler-community formation across the West. This does not imply every settler personally subscribed to Manifest Destiny, and the process also involved Indigenous dispossession and pre-existing Spanish, Mexican, Native, Black, and immigrant communities.
source_label: Library of Congress — Westward Expansion: Encounters at a Cultural Crossroads

note: The Hamilton family's settlement in the Salinas area is treated as a specific local case within the broader nineteenth-century process of western settler-community formation, rather than as a universal context node built around Steinbeck alone.
source_label: National Steinbeck Center — John Steinbeck biography

evidence: Farm Security Administration / Library of Congress documentation
note: 1930s Salinas is a specific case of large-scale commercial agriculture dependent on mobile and stratified labor. Farm Security Administration documentation describes concentrated grower-shippers, Mexican and Filipino field labor, white packing-shed labor, and workers following staggered harvests between valleys.
source_label: Library of Congress — Salinas Valley large-scale commercial agriculture, 1939

note: Hemingway's Kansas City Star newsroom is a specific instance of journalism functioning as writer formation: professional reporting practices, compression, observation, deadlines, and editorial conventions entered his early craft environment.

Clemens became a reporter at the Virginia City Territorial Enterprise, first used the Mark Twain name there, and went on to write thousands of newspaper and magazine pieces. Version 0.2 treats journalism as a reusable professional formation pattern while keeping Nevada-specific details in the evidence and narrower context nodes.
source_label: National Endowment for the Humanities — Documenting Mark Twain

note: García Márquez repeatedly described journalism as his central vocation and said the journalistic approach to reality remained the same across his journalism, literature, and political writing. This supports journalism as formation, not merely a side occupation.
source_label: Mexico Secretaría de Cultura — García Márquez on journalism
